§3.6.1 Do

§3.6.1.1 Write from inside the hiring manager's head, per §3.1.2, rather than from a checklist of categories to fill.
§3.6.1.2 Ground every grade boundary in the candidate's actual record, per §3.4.7.

A shorter rubric with honest gaps beats a padded one — eight vectors you can defend outrank fourteen where four have invented middles, because the invented four don't just fail to help, they blur the ten that would have worked.
§3.6.1.5 Honor the format contract at §3.2.1 in full.
§3.6.1.6 **State the hook first.** Before you write a single row for any vector, fix in your mind the JD-detectable hook that makes the vector gradeable, per §3.1.4. §3.6.1.7 **Echo the hook in X.** For every vector, the X row must name the JD signals the hook would require, using the same categories from the hook statement. If the hook was "The JD would signal distributed team leadership, e.g., 'global teams,' 'multiple time zones,' 'cross-regional coordination,' etc.," the X row should read: "The posting doesn't mention global teams, multiple time zones, cross-regional coordination, etc. — cannot grade."

§3.6.2 Don't

§3.6.2.1 Don't re-grade a question already covered by the drafted GET rubric at §3.4.9 and §2.9 — including under a new label. If a topic looks like it overlaps GET, don't just wave it through because the POV is technically different; earn the overlap. GET asks whether the resume signals the capability. DO asks whether Jolane actually has it. That's a real distinction only when your vector is grounded in something explicit and demonstrated in the profile — a documented outcome, a named engagement, a specific result — not in language that merely suggests or implies the capability without confirming it did happen. AI tooling and domain or sector fluency are where this keeps going wrong: a DO vector that just restates "the resume mentions this" in different words hasn't earned anything and should be dropped or merged back into GET's territory. One built on a specific, verifiable instance of Jolane actually doing the thing has earned its place.
§3.6.2.2 Don't grade paperwork or wording — that's GET's job. Don't grade feelings — that's LIKE's job. Don't grade terms — those belong to the filter stages.
§3.6.2.3 Don't grade from Jolane's side of the desk. A row must turn on what the hiring manager sees, gets, or loses — never on whether Jolane would be satisfied, stretched, bored, or under-used. "This role would waste her strength" is a candidate-satisfaction sentence wearing a DO grade; if a row would only bother her and not the manager, it isn't a DO row. Apply the Manager-Not-Candidate Test at §3.6.3.2 to every row, not just every vector. For D rows specifically: test every one against the "Wrong Tool, Not Broken Tool" rule. If the D row reads as "Jolane lacks capability X," rewrite it as "The role requires X in a context where Jolane's usual approach doesn't fit." The manager's frustration should come from *mismatch*, not deficiency.
§3.6.2.4 Don't produce vectors on topics owned elsewhere: remote or work-model policy, compensation, company size or stage, mission appeal, culture, titles, keywords or ATS behavior, growth trajectory. One exception: where the JD makes distributed or cross-timezone leadership part of the job itself, you may grade the candidate's demonstrated track record of doing that specific work — that's a capability vector about the candidate, not a policy vector about the company, so keep it framed that way or it collapses back into this rule.
§3.6.2.5 Don't write filler middles — "largely aligned," "partially matches." Filler is written in the same confident voice as real grounding, so nobody downstream can tell which vectors are load-bearing and which you improvised; use §3.6.1.4 instead.
§3.6.2.6 Don't write an F row. D is the floor. A low grade here is information for the candidate, not a verdict on the job — killing jobs belongs to the filter stages, which have already run by the time this rubric is applied.
§3.6.2.7 Don't cluster importance high, per §3.2.2.1.3 — if everything you've written lands at 8 or 10, you haven't actually discriminated between the vectors yet.
§3.6.2.8 Don't do math, and don't emit anything but the vectors, per §3.2.1.
§3.6.2.9 Don't write "the JD explicitly says" or "the JD describes." Write the scene itself, per §3.1.4 — and don't write a row that only works if a real JD confesses dysfunction it would never actually admit to; ground it in the euphemism or omission a real posting would use instead.

§3.6.3 Rejection Tests — apply every one of these to every vector before you keep it.

§3.6.3.1 Read-The-Work Test: could you grade this vector without reading a JD's account of the actual work? If yes, it's mispointed.
§3.6.3.2 Manager-Not-Candidate Test: does the grade turn on what the manager gets, or on what the candidate gets? Only the former belongs to this stage — see §3.6.2.3.
§3.6.3.3 Paper Test: would the grade change if the resume were reworded but the underlying track record stayed identical? If yes, it belongs to GET, not here.
§3.6.3.4 Priorities-Are-Evidence Test: if you catch yourself writing "they want...", stop — that's not this stage.
§3.6.3.5 **JD-Groundable Test:** Could a real JD, through its actual language or telling omissions, give Grace enough to pick a row? Before you write the vector, you must have already stated the JD-detectable hook (per §3.1.4). That hook must be:

- **Grounded in the candidate's material** — taken from §2.2, §2.3, §2.5, §2.6, §2.7, or §2.8 — not an invented requirement the candidate has no record for

- **Framed with "..., etc."** — so Grace knows to watch for the *category* of signal, not a verbatim match

If your row requires Grace to know a specific magnitude ("twelve time zones"), a hidden internal condition ("two executives with incompatible goals"), or an exact regulatory regime beyond what a JD would plausibly name, it fails. Real JDs don't reveal these. Drop the vector or reframe it around the hook you can actually state.
